enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's Names' permission to plead negligent misrepresentation
key_facts: Various Lloyd's Names sought permission to amend claims against Lloyd's to plead negligent misstatement and statutory misrepresentation relating to pre-1982 underwriting.
Most Names had previously been refused permission to amend; a narrowed group remained who relied on post-11 October 1981 brochure representations before 23 July 1982.
Lloyd's challenged the applications partly by reference to statutory demands and bankruptcy proceedings based on Equitas premium judgments.
The court assessed whether each Name had realistic prospects and whether any counterclaim could equal or exceed the statutory demand amount.
Only seven Names (Allard, Garrow, Hardman, Ranald, Remillard, Wilkinson and Woyka) were granted permission to amend.

enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend granted to seven Names only; refused for all other applicants, subject to costs following the event.
enrichment.ratio: Names may pursue negligent misrepresentation claims based on post-1981 Lloyd's brochure representations only if limitation under sections 14A and 14B of the Limitation Act 1980 permits and the proposed claim has realistic prospects, including on the figures where a counterclaim is relied on to defeat a statutory demand.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of IAT remittal in Turkish asylum appeal
key_facts: A Turkish Kurdish Alevi applicant claimed asylum based on persecution linked to Newroz celebrations, PKK association and coerced village guard service.
An adjudicator allowed the appeal on a reasonable-degree-of-likelihood basis, finding risk of arrest and torture on return.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal and remitted for rehearing, citing the Home Office's absence before the adjudicator and failure to consider internal relocation.
The High Court refused permission for judicial review of the remittal.
Laws LJ held the adjudicator failed to reconcile expert evidence (McDowall) with country information (CIPU), justifying IAT interference.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judicial review of refusal of permission to challenge an Immigration Appeal Tribunal remittal order.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's asylum decision may properly be interfered with where there is a defect of reasoning, such as failing to explain a conclusion on risk of return in light of conflicting country information and expert evidence; a party who did not appear before the adjudicator cannot ordinarily obtain remittal simply to ventilate matters that could have been raised there.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT had a proper basis to interfere with the adjudicator's determination
Effect of the Secretary of State's non-representation before the adjudicator
Internal relocation and village guard desertion in Turkish asylum cases
Standard and quality of reasoning required in asylum credibility findings

enrichment.short_title: Products liability cover for defective Eurostar glass panels
key_facts: Pilkington supplied heat-soaked toughened glass installed at the Eurostar terminal at Waterloo; a small number of panels later fractured in situ.
Eurostar incurred investigation and safety-remediation costs without removing the panels; Tarmac sought indemnity from Pilkington.
Pilkington claimed under a CGU Global Liability Policy covering physical damage to third-party property caused by supplied products.
The judge held installation of potentially defective panels did not itself constitute physical damage and that late notice breached a condition precedent.
The Court of Appeal upheld both conclusions and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court judgment on coverage and notice under a products liability policy.
enrichment.ratio: Under standard products liability wording, incorporation of a product that may fail in future does not amount to physical damage to the insured's property unless harmful physical alteration has occurred; notice-of-claim provisions may operate as conditions precedent to insurer liability even without prejudice to the insurer.
legal_issues: Whether installation of defective glass panels constituted physical damage to the terminal

enrichment.short_title: Section 55 asylum support and delay in claiming asylum
key_facts: Mr Wembo, a Congolese national, entered the UK on 4 May 2003 and claimed asylum in Liverpool on 8 May 2003.
The Secretary of State refused asylum support because the claim was not made as soon as reasonably practicable after arrival.
The claimant relied on agent instructions and on R (Q) v SSHD on the relevance of facilitators.
The decision letter challenged the credibility of his account of entry, passport use and failure to claim at the airport.
Newman J held the decision-maker was entitled to focus on credibility and that the agent factor did not require explicit mention on these facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of refusal of asylum support under section 55.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; claimant failed to discharge burden of showing asylum claimed at first reasonable opportunity.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 55 the burden rests on the applicant to show a claim was made as soon as reasonably practicable; while agent influence is a relevant factor under R (Q), it need not be expressly addressed where the interview and decision letter show the case turned on credibility of the claimant's own account.

enrichment.short_title: Sharia proviso in English-law Islamic finance agreements

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations

key_facts: Shamil Bank of Bahrain advanced funds to Beximco group companies under Morabaha and later Ijarah-style restructuring agreements totalling about US$49.7 million.
The agreements contained a governing law clause: subject to the principles of the Glorious Sharia'a, governed by English law.
Defendants argued transactions were disguised interest-bearing loans (Riba) and void under Sharia, defeating summary judgment.
Morison J held English law alone governed and granted summary judgment; permission to appeal was limited to the governing law clause.
The Court of Appeal held the Sharia reference did not incorporate Sharia as a parallel governing law or condition precedent and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment on debt and guarantee claims in Islamic finance litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; principal debtors and guarantors liable under English law.
enrichment.ratio: A clause making an agreement subject to the principles of Sharia but governed by English law does not incorporate Sharia as governing law or as a freestanding enforceability condition; under the Rome Convention parties may choose only the law of a country, and general Sharia references are insufficiently certain for incorporation by reference.
legal_issues: Construction of dual Sharia and English governing law clauses
Whether Sharia principles can be chosen as governing law under the Rome Convention

enrichment.short_title: School Sites Act reverter when trust purpose changed
key_facts: Land at St Philip's School, Maidstone was conveyed in 1866 on trust to educate poorer classes in the ecclesiastical district of St Philip and for no other purpose.
From the 1930s onward the school admitted many pupils outside the district and from other social classes, with no admissions restriction.
The first-instance judge found the school purpose had widened to educating all comers but held reverter had not occurred because two purposes coexisted.
The Court of Appeal held that finding was inconsistent: the original stipulated purpose had ceased long before 17 August 1975.
Automatic reverter under section 2 therefore occurred; trustees held proceeds as trustees of the 1866 deed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery Division declaration on whether land reverted under the School Sites Act 1841.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; reverter held to have occurred automatically and irrevocably before the Reverter of Sites Act 1987 cut-off for adverse possession.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 2 of the School Sites Act 1841, where land granted for a specified educational purpose is used for a materially different purpose—such as a general open-admission school rather than education of qualifying poor persons in the named district—the authorised purpose ceases and reverter is triggered, even if the institution continues operating as a school.
legal_issues: Meaning of cessation of purpose under section 2 School Sites Act 1841
Whether educating non-qualifying pupils alongside qualifying pupils prevents reverter
Interaction with Reverter of Sites Act 1987 and adverse possession
Construction of 'and for no other purpose' in Victorian school trust deeds

enrichment.short_title: Article 5(5) compensation after unlawful continued detention
key_facts: Mr Richards, a mandatory life prisoner, was not released until 12 August 2002 although his tariff expired on 19 September 2001 and the Parole Board recommended release on 16 November 2001.
He sought compensation for detention from November 2001 under Article 5(5) ECHR after the Secretary of State refused his claim.
Silber J held Article 5(5) can give a domestic right to compensation even where section 6 HRA does not, and that Stafford v UK could have retrospective effect.

Despite succeeding on those legal issues, the claim failed because the claimant could not establish loss: he would likely have remained detained in any event due to disability, behaviour and accommodation difficulties.
Judicial review of the refusal decision was dismissed with costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review and damages claim following refusal of compensation for post-tariff detention.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no compensation awarded despite favourable rulings on Article 5(5) and Stafford retrospectivity.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5(5) ECHR may provide a freestanding domestic right to compensation for unlawful detention not limited by section 6 HRA, and Strasbourg jurisprudence such as Stafford may apply retrospectively; however a claimant must still prove causation of loss and the court retains discretion to refuse compensation where detention would have continued in any event.
legal_issues: Retrospective effect of European Court of Human Rights decisions
Whether Article 5(5) creates an enforceable domestic compensation right
Relationship between Article 5(5) and sections 6 and 8 Human Rights Act 1998
Causation and discretion where Parole Board recommended release but prisoner remained detained

enrichment.short_title: Drink-driving blood sample continuity and late analyst evidence
key_facts: Mrs Khatibi was convicted by City of London magistrates of driving with excess alcohol after a blood sample showed 84 mg per 100 ml.
Defence challenged continuity of the blood sample, admissibility of the forensic analyst's evidence, and a five-month adjournment to call his assistant Debbie Kirkham.
Magistrates first retired on the continuity point only, then adjourned part-heard to hear Kirkham's evidence after R v Tate was cited.
Nelson J held the retirement was on a discrete issue, not a final verdict, so further prosecution evidence could be admitted.
The court upheld the conviction, finding sufficient inferential evidence linking the analysed sample to the defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case stated appeal to the Divisional Court from magistrates' drink-driving conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all three stated questions.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates may exercise discretion to reopen and adjourn before retiring on the whole case to call further straightforward forensic evidence; where label details align with police and medical evidence, continuity of a blood sample may be established by reasonable inference, including via sections 24 and 26 Criminal Justice Act 1988 if admissibility had been raised.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates could adjourn after partial retirement to call an assistant analyst
Fair trial and Article 6 implications of a five-month adjournment

enrichment.short_title: Kidnapping convictions quashed over co-accused lie and identification

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Collins and Keep were convicted of kidnapping Hutchinson and firearms offences linked to recovering stolen cannabis.
Hutchinson escaped to Dartford police station after being beaten and forced into car boots at gunpoint.
Collins appealed against admission of £10,300 cash found in the Audi and against use of a lie told by co-accused Burt to police.
The court quashed Collins' convictions because mere silence when Burt lied was insufficient and the Lucas direction was inadequate.
Keep's convictions were quashed because PC Parlour's 'looked like Keep' evidence required a Turnbull direction when used as supporting identification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Crown Court appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Collins convictions on counts 1 and 2 quashed; Keep convictions on counts 1 and 2 quashed; other grounds dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant's silence when a companion answers a police question with a lie cannot, without more, amount to adopting that lie as his own, particularly where parties are not on equal terms; where ostensibly non-identification evidence that someone looked like the accused is relied on to place him at the scene, a Turnbull warning is required.
legal_issues: Admissibility and use of cash evidence as corroboration in kidnapping prosecution
Whether silence can adopt a co-accused's lie to police (Christie, Hall, Chandler principles)
Adequacy of Lucas directions
Turnbull directions where witness says accused 'looked like' a known person

key_facts: Mr Griffin, aged 33, applied to Westminster as homeless with reactive depression and alcohol problems after leaving his mother's home.
The housing review officer applied the Pereira vulnerability test and decided he was not in priority need.
The county court judge held the officer applied too high a threshold by omitting a 'likely to suffer injury' formulation from the Code of Guidance.
Kennedy LJ held the review officer correctly applied Pereira and that introducing 'likely' from the code would wrongly dilute the statutory test.
The Secretary of State's appeal was allowed and the review decision restored.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal from a county court appeal under section 204 Housing Act 1996 on a point of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; review officer's decision that applicant lacked priority need restored.
enrichment.ratio: The vulnerability test under section 189(1)(c) Housing Act 1996 is whether, when homeless, the applicant would be less able to fend for himself than an ordinary homeless person so that injury or detriment will result; the Pereira formulation governs and the Code of Guidance's addition of 'likely to' does not alter the statutory test.
